Sam —

Appreciate the clear ask. High-level answers below + attached artifact (RTO-RPO-matrix.xlsx) and a short runbook snippet. Monica and Karthik are looped for technical specifics.

RTO / RPO (summary):
- Hosted API front-end (control plane + edge): target RTO = 1 minute for automatic edge failover; nominal availability target 99.99%.
- Inference runtime (GPU-backed): typical cold-to-warm failover ~5–15 minutes depending on KV cache state; our recommended SLO for multi-region failover is RTO <= 15 minutes for full traffic cutover.
- RPO: with continuous KV prefix caching + streaming replication between regions, we commit to RPO <= 1 second for supported customer workloads; for customers that opt out of cross-region replication we document RPO as "best effort" and provide expected loss window (minutes).
- Worst-case contractual commitment (if requested): we can provide a 4-hour RTO SLA for cross-region catastrophic failover with explicit acceptance in the SOW; that is for customers requiring contractual backstop beyond operational SLOs.

Architecture & sequencing (short):
- Active region runs the serving runtime; warm standby region maintains synced model artifacts, warmed container images, and near-live KV replica.
- Failover sequencing: health detect -> route-staging -> instance warm-up (GPU pool allocation) -> KV sync finalization -> DNS cutover + traffic ramp -> telemetry verification.

I've attached: RTO-RPO-matrix.xlsx and runbook-snippets.pdf (excerpts: failover sequencing + DNS steps). Also shared a Drive folder with fuller material: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1A2B3Cexample

Next steps:
- Karthik will provide a tight tech breakdown (expected time per step) and a rehearsal template.
- If Helix prefers a contractual RTO different to the operational SLOs we can capture that in the SOW/annex.

Sent from my mobile — will follow up with the technical note shortly.

Regards,

Sam / Alex —

Adding technical detail that you can paste into your internal questionnaire or BCP artifact. Below are expected per-step durations and failure modes. This is intended as a reproducible sequence you can test in a rehearsal.

1) Detection & gating (0–30s): health probes detect regional CI failures (HTTP code/latency, instance telemetry). We use distributed health checks; false-positive suppression window configurable.

2) Route staging (30s–2m): traffic split to degraded pool while warm standby continues warm-up. Our routing layer supports incremental ramping to avoid cold-thundering; typical ramp is 0 -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% over 2–5 minutes depending on endpoint criticality.

3) GPU pool allocation & KV finalization (2–12m): allocate reserved/burst GPUs in target region and finalize KV prefix sync. If model weights are cached, container start is fast (30–90s). If a cold artifact pull is required, additional minutes depend on network throughput; we recommend proactive artifact mirroring for SLAs <= 15m.

4) DNS cutover & edge scaling (15s–3m): once backend readiness gates pass we update routing (weighted DNS or global LB) and scale edge edge caches. DNS TTLs and route propagation are pre-negotiated in the runbook (we recommend TTL <= 60s for critical endpoints).

5) Post-failover verification (0–10m): smoke tests and data consistency checks; rollback hooks available.

Notes on RPO: our streaming replication for customer metadata and KV uses a near-synchronous replication path; for write-heavy workflows we advise extra verification steps. RPO <=1s assumes replication enabled and bandwidth commitments met.

Evidence we can provide:
- Runbook snippets (attached) mapping playbook steps to telemetry traces.
- Rehearsal logs for a prior customer rehearsal (sanitized).
- A rehearsal plan (calendar ICS) we can run jointly.

I'll attach the rehearsal template and a compressed snippet of the automated smoke-test that we run post-cutover.

—Karthik
Principal Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
karthik.iyer@redwood.com
